summary: Defines a Telnet option giving a mechanism for extending the set of possible options. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When you run out of room on a list, you add a second page. This option adds more room for Telnet features.

questions: how to add more telnet options
what is telnet extended options list
how many telnet options are there
subtitle: A Telnet option that reserves option number 255 so the 256-entry option list can later be extended.

tldr.problem: Telnet option numbers fit in one byte, so eventually a 257th option will be needed.
tldr.mechanism: The EXTENDED-OPTIONS-LIST option (EXOPL, code 255) reserves that number now and defines subcommands that negotiate a second list of options inside Telnet subnegotiation.
tldr.outcome: Negotiating options on the Extended Options List is not permitted unless both sides agree to EXOPL, which is off by default.

today: RFC 861 is an Internet Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Reserving Option 255
sections.content:
Eventually a 257th Telnet option will be needed. The EXTENDED-OPTIONS-LIST option (EXOPL) will extend the option list by another 256 options in a way that is easy to implement.

The RFC proposes it now, rather than much later, in order to reserve the option number 255.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet only has room for so many features. This saves a spot now so it can add many more later.

sections.title: Turning Extended Options On
sections.content:
EXOPL is negotiated with the usual commands. IAC DO EXOPL requests, or confirms, that the receiver will negotiate options on the Extended Options List. IAC WILL EXOPL asks permission to do so, or confirms it will. IAC WON'T EXOPL refuses to negotiate or continue, and IAC DON'T EXOPL demands that no further negotiation of such options take place.

The default is WON'T EXOPL and DON'T EXOPL: negotiation of options on the Extended Options List is not permitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Both computers must say yes before they can use the second page of features. Without a yes, they stay on page one.

sections.title: Subcommand Format
sections.content:
EXOPL has five subcommand codes: WILL, WON'T, DO, DON'T and SB. They mean exactly what the Telnet commands of those names mean. For consistency they use the same values as the Telnet command codes, 250-254.

Once both sides have agreed to EXOPL, negotiating a specific extended option looks like IAC SB EXOPL DO/DON'T/WILL/WON'T/<option code> IAC SE. If that option then needs subnegotiation, the format is IAC SB EXOPL SB <option code> <parameters> SE IAC SE.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra features are asked for in a message inside another message, like a note tucked in an envelope.
